chapterTitle: The Day of the Lord and the God Who Waits
themeTitle: “The Lord Is Not Slow Concerning His Promise … But Is Patient with Us”

scripture.text: This is now, beloved, the second letter that I have written to you; and in both of them I stir up your sincere mind by reminding you;
scripture.understanding: ταύτην ἤδη, ἀγαπητοί, δευτέραν ὑμῖν γράφω ἐπιστολήν, “This is now, beloved, the second letter that I have written to you” — ἀγαπητός, from the love family, used four times in this chapter; δεύτερος, second, most naturally referring to 1 Peter. ἐν αἷς διεγείρω ὑμῶν ἐν ὑπομνήσει τὴν εἰλικρινῆ διάνοιαν, “and in both of them I stir up your sincere mind by reminding you” — διεγείρω, to wake fully, as in 1:13; εἰλικρινής, pure, tested in the sunlight; διάνοια, the thinking mind of 1 Peter 1:13.

scripture.text: that you should remember the words which were spoken before by the holy prophets, and the commandment of us, the apostles of the Lord and Savior:
scripture.understanding: μνησθῆναι τῶν προειρημένων ῥημάτων ὑπὸ τῶν ἁγίων προφητῶν, “that you should remember the words which were spoken before by the holy prophets” — ῥῆμα, from the word family: particular spoken words, as distinct from λόγος, the whole message (v. 5). καὶ τῆς τῶν ἀποστόλων ὑμῶν ἐντολῆς τοῦ κυρίου καὶ σωτῆρος, “and the commandment of us, the apostles of the Lord and Savior” — Old Testament prophets and New Testament apostles stand side by side as the voice of God (Ephesians 2:20). ἅγιος is from the holy family — holy, set apart for God; as a noun, the saints — God’s holy people.

scripture.text: knowing this first, that in the last days mockers will come, walking after their own lusts,
scripture.understanding: τοῦτο πρῶτον γινώσκοντες, “knowing this first” — γινώσκω, from the know family, the same opening as 1:20. ὅτι ἐλεύσονται ἐπ᾽ ἐσχάτων τῶν ἡμερῶν ἐμπαῖκται, “that in the last days mockers will come” — ἡμέρα, from the time family: the last days began with Christ's first coming (Acts 2:17); ἐμπαίκτης, a scoffer, one who treats holy things as a joke. κατὰ τὰς ἰδίας ἐπιθυμίας αὐτῶν πορευόμενοι, “walking after their own lusts” — the root of their scoffing is moral: denying judgement frees them to follow desire.

scripture.text: and saying, “Where is the promise of his coming? For, from the day that the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were from the beginning of the creation.”
scripture.understanding: καὶ λέγοντες, “and saying, ‘Where is the promise of his coming?’” — ἐπαγγελία, a promise; παρουσία, Christ's royal arrival, the coming Peter saw previewed on the mountain (1:16). “For, from the day that the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were from the beginning of the creation.” — κοιμάω, from the sleep family: the believer's word for death; διαμένω, to remain unchanged; ἀρχή, beginning — the word is also in the power family, where it means rule or principality, but here it carries its first sense, the start; κτίσις, creation. Their argument: the universe is a closed system; nothing ever breaks in.

scripture.text: For this they willfully forget, that there were heavens from of old, and an earth formed out of water and amid water, by the word of God;
scripture.understanding: λανθάνει γὰρ αὐτοὺς τοῦτο θέλοντας, “For this they willfully forget” — λανθάνω, to escape notice; θέλω, by choice. Their ignorance is deliberate. ὅτι οὐρανοὶ ἦσαν ἔκπαλαι καὶ γῆ ἐξ ὕδατος καὶ δι᾽ ὕδατος συνεστῶσα, “that there were heavens from of old, and an earth formed out of water and amid water” — γῆ, from the world family: the earth, the land; συνίστημι, to hold together (Genesis 1:6–9). τῷ τοῦ θεοῦ λόγῳ, “by the word of God” — λόγος, from the word family: God's creative command. The world has not continued unchanged; God made it by His word, and God has intervened before.

scripture.text: by which means the world that then was, being overflowed with water, perished.
scripture.understanding: δι᾽ ὧν ὁ τότε κόσμος ὕδατι κατακλυσθεὶς ἀπώλετο, “by which means the world that then was, being overflowed with water, perished” — κόσμος, from the world family: the ordered world of human life, as distinct from γῆ in verse 5, the physical earth. κατακλύζω, to flood, the verb of the κατακλυσμός of 2:5; ἀπόλλυμι, to perish. Water and word made the world; water and word judged it.

scripture.text: But the heavens that now exist, and the earth, by the same word have been stored up for fire, being reserved against the day of judgment and destruction of ungodly men.
scripture.understanding: οἱ δὲ νῦν οὐρανοὶ καὶ ἡ γῆ τῷ αὐτῷ λόγῳ τεθησαυρισμένοι εἰσὶν πυρί, “But the heavens that now exist, and the earth, by the same word have been stored up for fire” — λόγος, from the word family: the same word that created and flooded; θησαυρίζω, to store up as treasure, the verb of James 5:3. γῆ, from the world family. τηρούμενοι εἰς ἡμέραν κρίσεως καὶ ἀπωλείας τῶν ἀσεβῶν ἀνθρώπων, “being reserved against the day of judgment and destruction of ungodly men” — τηρέω, from the hold family: kept, like the fallen angels (2:4); ἡμέρα, from the time family; ἀσεβής, from the godliness family. Flood then; fire next. κρίσις is from the judge family — judgement as an act or process — the trial, the hour of judging.

scripture.text: But don’t forget this one thing, beloved, that one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day.
scripture.understanding: ἓν δὲ τοῦτο μὴ λανθανέτω ὑμᾶς, ἀγαπητοί, “But don’t forget this one thing, beloved” — ἀγαπητός, from the love family; λανθάνω, the same verb as verse 5: the scoffers forget deliberately; believers must not forget at all. ὅτι μία ἡμέρα παρὰ κυρίῳ ὡς χίλια ἔτη καὶ χίλια ἔτη ὡς ἡμέρα μία, “that one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day” — echoing Psalm 90:4. ἡμέρα and ἔτος, both from the time family: God is not bound by time as we are. A thousand years do not tire Him, and a single day is enough for Him to do what centuries could not.

scripture.text: The Lord is not slow concerning his promise, as some count slowness; but is patient with us, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance.
scripture.understanding: οὐ βραδύνει κύριος τῆς ἐπαγγελίας, “The Lord is not slow concerning his promise” — βραδύνω, to delay, the verb of James's ‘slow to speak’ (James 1:19). ὥς τινες βραδύτητα ἡγοῦνται, “as some count slowness” — ἡγέομαι, to reckon. ἀλλὰ μακροθυμεῖ εἰς ὑμᾶς, “but is patient with us” — μακροθυμέω, from the endurance family: long-tempered, the patience God showed in Noah's day (1 Peter 3:20). μὴ βουλόμενός τινας ἀπολέσθαι, “not wishing that any should perish” — βούλομαι, to desire. ἀλλὰ πάντας εἰς μετάνοιαν χωρῆσαι, “but that all should come to repentance” — μετάνοια, a change of mind and direction. God's delay is mercy, giving time to turn (1 Timothy 2:4). How this desire relates to God's choosing is debated; Peter's point is that God takes no pleasure in destruction.

scripture.text: But the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night; in which the heavens will pass away with a great noise, and the elements will be dissolved with fervent heat, and the earth and the works that are in it will be burned up.
scripture.understanding: ἥξει δὲ ἡμέρα κυρίου ὡς κλέπτης, “But the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night” — ἡμέρα, from the time family: the day of the Lord, the Old Testament's great day of judgement; κλέπτης, a thief: unexpected, as Jesus said (Matthew 24:43). ἐν ᾗ οἱ οὐρανοὶ ῥοιζηδὸν παρελεύσονται, “in which the heavens will pass away with a great noise” — ῥοιζηδόν, with a rushing roar, the whoosh of a fire or a storm; παρέρχομαι, the ‘pass away’ of James 1:10. στοιχεῖα δὲ καυσούμενα λυθήσεται, “and the elements will be dissolved with fervent heat” — στοιχεῖον, the basic elements, or perhaps the heavenly bodies; λύω, to loosen, dissolve. “and the earth and the works that are in it will be burned up” — γῆ, from the world family; ἔργον, from the work family. The WEB follows manuscripts reading κατακαήσεται, ‘burned up’; the oldest read εὑρεθήσεται, ‘will be found’, laid bare before God. Either way, nothing will be hidden.

scripture.text: Therefore since all these things will be destroyed like this, what kind of people ought you to be in holy living and godliness,
scripture.understanding: τούτων οὖν πάντων λυομένων, “Therefore since all these things will be destroyed like this” — λύω again, dissolved. ποταποὺς δεῖ ὑπάρχειν ὑμᾶς, “what kind of people ought you to be” — ποταπός, of what sort. Peter's eschatology is always ethical: knowing the end shapes how you live now. ἐν ἁγίαις ἀναστροφαῖς καὶ εὐσεβείαις, “in holy living and godliness” — both plural in Greek, ‘holy ways of life and acts of godliness’; ἅγιος, the holiness of 1 Peter 1:15; εὐσέβεια, from the godliness family, the godliness of 1:3, 6–7. ἅγιος is from the holy family — holy, set apart for God; as a noun, the saints — God’s holy people.

scripture.text: looking for and earnestly desiring the coming of the day of God, which will cause the burning heavens to be dissolved, and the elements will melt with fervent heat?
scripture.understanding: προσδοκῶντας καὶ σπεύδοντας τὴν παρουσίαν τῆς τοῦ θεοῦ ἡμέρας, “looking for and earnestly desiring the coming of the day of God” — προσδοκάω, to wait expectantly; σπεύδω, to hurry, to hasten, or to long for: believers may even ‘hasten’ the day by holy living, prayer and witness, since God waits for repentance (v. 9). παρουσία, the coming; ἡμέρα, from the time family. δι᾽ ἣν οὐρανοὶ πυρούμενοι λυθήσονται καὶ στοιχεῖα καυσούμενα τήκεται, “which will cause the burning heavens to be dissolved, and the elements will melt with fervent heat?” — πυρόω, to set on fire; τήκω, to melt, as wax melts (Isaiah 34:4).

scripture.text: But, according to his promise, we look for new heavens and a new earth, in which righteousness dwells.
scripture.understanding: καινοὺς δὲ οὐρανοὺς καὶ γῆν καινὴν κατὰ τὸ ἐπάγγελμα αὐτοῦ προσδοκῶμεν, “But, according to his promise, we look for new heavens and a new earth” — καινός, from the new family: new in kind and quality, renewed, not merely νέος, new in time. The promise of Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22. γῆ, from the world family. ἐν οἷς δικαιοσύνη κατοικεῖ, “in which righteousness dwells” — κατοικέω, to settle down and live permanently. In this world righteousness is a stranger, like Lot in Sodom (2:8); in the new creation it is at home.

scripture.text: Therefore, beloved, seeing that you look for these things, be diligent to be found in peace, without defect and blameless in his sight.
scripture.understanding: διό, ἀγαπητοί, ταῦτα προσδοκῶντες, “Therefore, beloved, seeing that you look for these things” — ἀγαπητός, from the love family. σπουδάσατε, “be diligent” — σπουδάζω, the word of 1:10 and 1:15. ἄσπιλοι καὶ ἀμώμητοι αὐτῷ εὑρεθῆναι ἐν εἰρήνῃ, “to be found in peace, without defect and blameless in his sight” — ἄσπιλος, without spot, the word for Christ the spotless Lamb (1 Peter 1:19) and the exact opposite of the false teachers, ‘spots and defects’ (2:13); ἀμώμητος, without blame. εἰρήνη, peace with God and with others. Hope purifies (1 John 3:3).

scripture.text: Regard the patience of our Lord as salvation; even as our beloved brother Paul also, according to the wisdom given to him, wrote to you;
scripture.understanding: καὶ τὴν τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν μακροθυμίαν σωτηρίαν ἡγεῖσθε, “Regard the patience of our Lord as salvation” — μακροθυμία, from the endurance family, as in verse 9: every day of delay is another day of opportunity to be saved; σωτηρία, salvation. καθὼς καὶ ὁ ἀγαπητὸς ἡμῶν ἀδελφὸς Παῦλος, “even as our beloved brother Paul also” — ἀγαπητός, from the love family: the man who once rebuked Peter to his face (Galatians 2:11) he now calls ‘beloved brother’. κατὰ τὴν δοθεῖσαν αὐτῷ σοφίαν ἔγραψεν ὑμῖν, “according to the wisdom given to him, wrote to you” — σοφία, from the wisdom family: a gift from God (James 1:5).

scripture.text: as also in all of his letters, speaking in them of these things. In those, there are some things that are hard to understand, which the ignorant and unsettled twist, as they also do to the other Scriptures, to their own destruction.
scripture.understanding: ὡς καὶ ἐν πάσαις ταῖς ἐπιστολαῖς, “as also in all of his letters” — Peter knows a collection of Paul's letters. ἐν αἷς ἐστιν δυσνόητά τινα, “In those, there are some things that are hard to understand” — δυσνόητος, difficult to grasp: even an apostle found Paul hard at times. ἃ οἱ ἀμαθεῖς καὶ ἀστήρικτοι στρεβλοῦσιν, “which the ignorant and unsettled twist” — ἀμαθής, untaught; ἀστήρικτος, unstable, the word of 2:14; στρεβλόω, to wrench, as on a rack. ὡς καὶ τὰς λοιπὰς γραφάς, “as they also do to the other Scriptures” — γραφή: Peter places Paul's letters alongside the Scriptures, a striking witness to their authority. πρὸς τὴν ἰδίαν αὐτῶν ἀπώλειαν, “to their own destruction.”

scripture.text: You therefore, beloved, knowing these things beforehand, beware, lest being carried away with the error of the wicked, you fall from your own steadfastness.
scripture.understanding: ὑμεῖς οὖν, ἀγαπητοί, προγινώσκοντες, “You therefore, beloved, knowing these things beforehand” — ἀγαπητός, from the love family, a fourth time; προγινώσκω, to know in advance: forewarned is forearmed. φυλάσσεσθε, “beware” — φυλάσσω, from the hold family: guard yourselves, the word used of God guarding Noah (2:5). ἵνα μὴ τῇ τῶν ἀθέσμων πλάνῃ συναπαχθέντες, “lest being carried away with the error of the wicked” — ἄθεσμος, lawless, the word of 2:7; πλάνη, error; συναπάγω, to be swept away together, as Barnabas was ‘carried away’ (Galatians 2:13). ἐκπέσητε τοῦ ἰδίου στηριγμοῦ, “you fall from your own steadfastness” — ἐκπίπτω, to fall off, like the flower of 1 Peter 1:24; στηριγμός, firm footing, the noun of στηρίζω (1:12) and the opposite of ἀστήρικτος (v. 16).

scripture.text: But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To him be the glory both now and forever. Amen.
scripture.understanding: αὐξάνετε δὲ ἐν χάριτι καὶ γνώσει τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν καὶ σωτῆρος Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, “But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ” — αὐξάνω, to grow, the word of 1 Peter 2:2: newborns growing by the word. γνῶσις, from the know family, as in 1:5–6. The defence against falling is not standing still but growing. αὐτῷ ἡ δόξα καὶ νῦν καὶ εἰς ἡμέραν αἰῶνος, “To him be the glory both now and forever” — literally ‘to the day of the age’: ἡμέρα, from the time family, and αἰών, in the time family and the world family, the endless day that dawns when the morning star rises (1:19). Glory is given to Jesus as to God. Ἀμήν. These are among the last recorded words of Peter.

visualMeditations.title: The Scoffers' Closed Box
visualMeditations.image: Picture a group of men sitting comfortably in a sealed room, sure that nothing outside can affect them. ‘Nothing has changed since our grandfathers,’ they laugh. ‘The sun rises, the seasons turn, people are born and die. All this talk of a coming King is a fairy tale.’ Outside the room, unseen, the water once rose to the rooftops; and now a fire is being gathered.
visualMeditations.meaning: “Where is the promise of his coming? For, from the day that the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were from the beginning of the creation” (v. 4). But they forget on purpose that God created the world by His word and once judged it by water. “But the heavens that now exist, and the earth, by the same word have been stored up for fire, being reserved against the day of judgment and destruction of ungodly men” (v. 7). The world is not a closed box. God has broken in before, and He will again.

visualMeditations.title: The Patient Father at the Door
visualMeditations.image: Picture a father standing at the door of his house every evening, looking down the road. His son left years ago. Neighbours say he should give up and lock the door. But each night he waits a little longer, leaving the lamp burning, because he does not want his son to come home to a closed house.
visualMeditations.meaning: “The Lord is not slow concerning his promise, as some count slowness; but is patient with us, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance” (v. 9). What looks like delay is mercy. Every day the Lord does not return is another day for someone to come home. “Regard the patience of our Lord as salvation” (v. 15).

visualMeditations.title: The Thief in the Night
visualMeditations.image: Picture a house asleep at three in the morning. No alarm, no warning — just a sudden crash, and everything changes. Then picture the whole sky lit with fire, the roar of the heavens passing away, the elements melting like wax, and every work of humankind laid bare.
visualMeditations.meaning: “But the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night; in which the heavens will pass away with a great noise, and the elements will be dissolved with fervent heat, and the earth and the works that are in it will be burned up” (v. 10). Peter's question follows immediately: “Therefore since all these things will be destroyed like this, what kind of people ought you to be in holy living and godliness” (v. 11). Knowing the end changes how you live today.

visualMeditations.title: Where Righteousness Is at Home
visualMeditations.image: Picture a refugee who has lived for years as a stranger — never quite fitting in, always slightly afraid, grieved by the injustice around him. One day he is given the keys to a house in a new country where justice is the law of the land, where no one is oppressed, and where he finally belongs. He walks through the door and weeps.
visualMeditations.meaning: “But, according to his promise, we look for new heavens and a new earth, in which righteousness dwells” (v. 13). Here, righteousness is a foreigner, like Lot in Sodom. There, it will be at home. “Therefore, beloved, seeing that you look for these things, be diligent to be found in peace, without defect and blameless in his sight” (v. 14). Live now as citizens of the world that is coming.

structure.label: Remember the Word (v. 1-2)
structure.body: In this second letter Peter stirs up their sincere minds to remember the words of the holy prophets and the command of the Lord given through the apostles.

structure.label: The Scoffers Answered (v. 3-7)
structure.body: In the last days scoffers will come, following their own desires and mocking the promise of Christ's coming, claiming everything continues unchanged; but they deliberately forget that God made the world by His word and destroyed it with water, and by the same word the present heavens and earth are reserved for fire on the day of judgement.

structure.label: God's Timing and Patience (v. 8-10)
structure.body: With the Lord one day is as a thousand years and a thousand years as one day; He is not slow but patient, not wanting anyone to perish but all to come to repentance; yet the day of the Lord will come like a thief, when the heavens pass away, the elements dissolve and the earth and its works are exposed.

structure.label: Living in the Light of the End (v. 11-16)
structure.body: Since everything will be dissolved, live in holiness and godliness, waiting for and hastening the day of God, looking for new heavens and a new earth where righteousness lives; be diligent to be found spotless and at peace, counting the Lord's patience as salvation, as Paul also wrote, though some of his writings are hard and are twisted by the unstable, as they twist the other Scriptures.

structure.label: Final Warning and Doxology (v. 17-18)
structure.body: Being forewarned, guard yourselves so as not to be carried away by the error of the lawless and lose your stability; grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, to whom be glory now and forever.

sections.heading: Where Is the Promise?
paragraphs: Peter's last chapter answers the scoffers. He reminds his readers of “the words which were spoken before by the holy prophets, and the commandment of us, the apostles of the Lord and Savior” (v. 2), and warns that “in the last days mockers will come, walking after their own lusts” (v. 3). Their question sounds reasonable: “Where is the promise of his coming? For, from the day that the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were from the beginning of the creation” (v. 4). Jesus had warned of the servant who says, “My lord is delaying his coming” (Matthew 24:48).

Peter exposes two things. First, their motive: they walk after their own desires. Denying a future judgement is convenient for those who want to live without accountability. Second, their selective memory: “For this they willfully forget” (v. 5). The world has not continued unchanged. It was made by God's word, and it was flooded by God's judgement in Noah's day (v. 6). The God who created and judged the world by His word has reserved the present heavens and earth “for fire, being reserved against the day of judgment and destruction of ungodly men” (v. 7).

Peter's argument is a lesson in how to answer doubt. He does not ignore the question. He goes back to what God has already done in history — creation and the flood — and shows that the same word that did those things has promised the next. History is not a closed circle; it is a story with a Creator, a judgement and a coming King.

sections.heading: God's Time and God's Patience
paragraphs: Then Peter turns to believers who may be troubled by the delay: “But don’t forget this one thing, beloved, that one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day” (v. 8). God does not experience time as we do. What seems long to us is not long to Him, and He can accomplish in a day what we could not in centuries.

More importantly, the delay has a purpose: “The Lord is not slow concerning his promise, as some count slowness; but is patient with us, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance” (v. 9). God's delay is His patience. Paul says the same: “Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, forbearance, and patience, not knowing that the goodness of God leads you to repentance?” (Romans 2:4), and God “desires all people to be saved and come to full knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2:4). Christians differ on how God's desire for all to repent relates to His choosing of His people; Peter's point is plain: God takes no pleasure in anyone's destruction, and every day of delay is a gift.

But patience is not cancellation. “But the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night” (v. 10). Jesus used the same image: “But know this, that if the master of the house had known in what watch of the night the thief was coming, he would have watched” (Matthew 24:43). Paul too: “For you yourselves know well that the day of the Lord comes like a thief in the night” (1 Thessalonians 5:2). The heavens will pass away, the elements dissolve, and the earth and all human works will be exposed — burned up, or ‘found out’, as the oldest manuscripts read. Nothing will be hidden.

sections.heading: What Kind of People Ought You to Be?
paragraphs: Peter never teaches about the end without applying it to the present. “Therefore since all these things will be destroyed like this, what kind of people ought you to be in holy living and godliness” (v. 11). If everything you can see will be dissolved, it is foolish to live for what you can see. The question is not ‘When will the end come?’ but ‘What kind of person will I be when it does?’

Believers are “looking for and earnestly desiring the coming of the day of God” (v. 12). The word σπεύδω can mean ‘eagerly desiring’ or ‘hastening’. Since God waits for repentance, the church's holiness, prayer and witness are in some sense bound up with the timing of the end. And they look not for destruction alone but for renewal: “But, according to his promise, we look for new heavens and a new earth, in which righteousness dwells” (v. 13). John saw it: “I saw a new heaven and a new earth: for the first heaven and the first earth have passed away, and the sea is no more” (Revelation 21:1). Paul says creation itself “will be delivered from the bondage of decay into the liberty of the glory of the children of God” (Romans 8:21).

So Peter calls for diligent holiness: “Therefore, beloved, seeing that you look for these things, be diligent to be found in peace, without defect and blameless in his sight” (v. 14). The false teachers were ‘spots and defects’ (2:13); believers are to be spotless like their Lord. John adds, “Everyone who has this hope set on him purifies himself, even as he is pure” (1 John 3:3). Hope does not make Christians passive; it makes them holy.

sections.heading: Paul, the Scriptures, and the Last Word
paragraphs: Peter adds a remarkable testimony to Paul: “even as our beloved brother Paul also, according to the wisdom given to him, wrote to you” (v. 15). The two apostles had once clashed at Antioch, when Paul “resisted him to his face” (Galatians 2:11). Now Peter calls him ‘beloved brother’ and honours his God-given wisdom. He even admits that Paul's letters contain “some things that are hard to understand, which the ignorant and unsettled twist, as they also do to the other Scriptures, to their own destruction” (v. 16). By saying ‘the other Scriptures’, Peter places Paul's letters alongside the Old Testament as the word of God.

His final warning gathers the whole letter: “You therefore, beloved, knowing these things beforehand, beware, lest being carried away with the error of the wicked, you fall from your own steadfastness” (v. 17). The unstable twist Scripture; the stable stand firm. The word for ‘steadfastness’ comes from the same root as ‘established’ (1:12) — the word Jesus used when He told Peter to strengthen his brothers.

And his very last words are a command and a doxology: “But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To him be the glory both now and forever. Amen” (v. 18). The letter began with grace and peace multiplied in the knowledge of God (1:2); it ends with grace and knowledge growing. The defence against error is not merely knowing what is false, but growing in Christ. And the final glory goes to Jesus — the same glory Peter saw on the mountain.

ntConnection.heading: The Thief, the New Creation and the Unshakeable Kingdom
paragraphs: Jesus promised that His words would outlast the universe: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matthew 24:35). Peter shows the same: the present heavens and earth are kept by God's word for judgement, but His promise of a new creation stands. Hebrews says, “Yet once more I will shake not only the earth, but also the heavens” (Hebrews 12:26), and explains that this signifies “the removing of those things that are shaken, as of things that have been made, that those things which are not shaken may remain” (Hebrews 12:27).

The new heavens and new earth of verse 13 are the climax of Revelation: “I saw a new heaven and a new earth: for the first heaven and the first earth have passed away, and the sea is no more” (Revelation 21:1), and “He will wipe away every tear from their eyes. Death will be no more; neither will there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain, any more. The first things have passed away” (Revelation 21:4). The risen Christ also warned, “If therefore you won’t watch, I will come as a thief, and you won’t know what hour I will come upon you” (Revelation 3:3).

Peter's call to holy living in view of the end echoes Paul: we are to live “soberly, righteously, and godly in this present age” (Titus 2:12), “looking for the blessed hope and appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ” (Titus 2:13). “For our citizenship is in heaven, from where we also wait for a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ” (Philippians 3:20). Peter's last letter ends where the whole New Testament points: grow in Christ while you wait for Him.

lexicon.insight: Strong's: “a derider, i.e. (by implication) a false teacher.” ἐμπαίκτης comes from ἐμπαίζω, to mock, the word used of the soldiers mocking Jesus. Jude uses it of the same people (Jude 18). The dictionary's note is revealing: scoffing and false teaching go together. The scoffers in Peter's day mocked the promise of Christ's return; their descendants still do. Peter says their scoffing grows from their desires: if there is no coming Judge, they can live as they like.

Strong's: “to be long-spirited, i.e. (objectively) forbearing or (subjectively) patient.” μακροθυμέω and μακροθυμία, from the endurance family, describe God's long temper — His refusal to act in quick anger. James used it of the farmer waiting for rain (James 5:7); Peter uses it of God waiting for sinners. Paul writes that God “endured with much patience vessels of wrath” (Romans 9:22). God's patience is not weakness or forgetfulness. It is mercy holding back judgement so that more can be saved.

Strong's derivation: ‘new (especially in freshness)’, while νέος is new ‘with respect to age’. καινός, from the new family, means new in kind and quality — renewed, fresh, different — as distinct from νέος, new in time. The new heavens and new earth are not simply a second universe made from nothing, but creation renewed and set free (Romans 8:21). It is the same word as the ‘new covenant’, the ‘new creation’ (2 Corinthians 5:17) and ‘Behold, I am making all things new’ (Revelation 21:5).

Strong's: “to "speed" ("study"), i.e. urge on (diligently or earnestly); by implication, to await eagerly”. σπεύδω means to hurry. It can be used of eager longing, as the WEB has it, or of actively hastening something. Since God delays the end to allow repentance (v. 9), the church's holiness, prayer (‘Your kingdom come’) and witness may in some sense hasten the day. Either way, believers do not merely wait passively; they wait with eagerness that shapes their lives.

Strong's: “stability (figuratively).” στηριγμός is the noun of στηρίζω, to establish, the word Jesus used when He told Peter to strengthen his brothers (Luke 22:32), and which Peter used of believers ‘established in the present truth’ (1:12). Its opposite, ἀστήρικτος, ‘unstable’, describes the souls false teachers entice (2:14) and those who twist Scripture (3:16). Peter's last letter is his final act of establishing the brothers — and the way to keep your footing is to grow.

holySpiritRevelation.intro: In this final chapter the Holy Spirit lifts your eyes to the end of history — and asks what kind of person you are becoming while you wait.

items.title: Have You Stopped Expecting Him?
items.body: The scoffers say nothing changes. Many believers do not mock, but they quietly stop expecting Christ to return. The Spirit asks: do you live as though this world is permanent? “But the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night” (v. 10). What would change in your priorities, spending and relationships if you truly expected Him?

items.title: Who Is God Waiting For?
items.body: God's patience is “not wishing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance” (v. 9). The Spirit brings someone to mind who has not yet come to Christ. Every day of delay is a day of mercy for them. Will you pray for them by name, and look for an opportunity to speak to them of the hope you have?

items.title: Are You Still Growing?
items.body: Peter's last words are “grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ” (v. 18). The Spirit wants to keep you steady — not by making you rigid, but by making you grow. Where are you standing still? Ask Him to show you the next step of growth in grace and in knowing Christ.

audit.title: The Expectation Check
audit.body: How often do you think about Christ's return? Does it shape your choices, or is it only a doctrine you agree with (vv. 10–12)?

audit.title: The Holiness Check
audit.body: If the Lord came today, would He find you ‘in peace, without defect and blameless’ (v. 14)? What needs to be put right before then?

audit.title: The Stability Check
audit.body: Are you easily carried away by new teachings, trends or arguments (v. 17)? How firmly are you rooted in Scripture — including the hard parts (v. 16)?

practices.title: Live in the Light of the Day
practices.body: Each morning this week, before you plan your day, read verses 10–14 and ask: ‘Lord, what kind of person ought I to be today?’ Choose one concrete act of holiness or godliness for that day — a temptation to refuse, a wrong to put right, a kindness to show. In the evening, thank God that His patience is still giving you time.

practices.title: Pray for the Ones He Is Waiting For
practices.body: Write down the names of three people who do not yet know Christ. Each day this month, pray verse 9 over them: ‘Lord, You are not willing that they should perish. Bring them to repentance.’ Ask God for one opportunity to share the hope of the new heavens and new earth with one of them.

prayerReflection: “Lord Jesus, I remember the words of the holy prophets and the commands You gave through Your apostles. In a world that mocks Your coming, keep me from forgetting what You have done — You made the world by Your word, You judged it in the flood, and by the same word You have reserved this world for the day of judgement. Thank You that You are not slow, but patient, not wanting anyone to perish but all to come to repentance. Let me count Your patience as salvation, and use every day of it well. I know that Your day will come like a thief in the night. So make me the kind of person I ought to be — holy in my living and godly in my ways. Make me eager for Your coming, and let my life hasten it. I look for new heavens and a new earth, where righteousness is at home. Make me diligent to be found by You in peace, spotless and blameless. Guard me from being carried away by the error of the lawless, and keep my footing firm. Thank You for the Scriptures, including the letters of Your servant Paul. Help me never to twist them, but to grow in Your grace and in knowing You, my Lord and Saviour. To You be the glory, now and to the day of eternity. Amen.”

storyConnections.title: The Flood: Water, Word and Judgement
storyConnections.summary: In the beginning God spoke, and the waters were separated, and dry land appeared — a world formed out of water and by water through His word. Centuries later, when wickedness filled the earth, the same God opened the fountains of the deep and the windows of heaven, and the waters covered even the mountains. Everything outside the ark perished. The scoffers in Peter's day claimed nothing ever changes. Peter points them to the flood: the God who spoke the world into being has already judged it once, and His word has reserved the present world for fire.

storyConnections.title: The Faithful and Wicked Servants
storyConnections.summary: Jesus told of a master who left his servants in charge of his household. The faithful servant kept working and caring for the household, ready for his master's return at any time. The wicked servant said in his heart, “My lord is delaying his coming” (Matthew 24:48), and began to beat his fellow servants and eat and drink with drunkards. The master came on a day he did not expect and at an hour he did not know. Peter's scoffers are that wicked servant: they mistake delay for absence. Peter calls believers to be the faithful servant, living in holiness and peace whenever He comes.

storyConnections.title: Peter and Paul at Antioch
storyConnections.summary: At Antioch, Paul confronted Peter publicly for withdrawing from Gentile believers when men came from Jerusalem: “But when Peter came to Antioch, I resisted him to his face, because he stood condemned” (Galatians 2:11). It was a painful moment between two great apostles. Yet at the Jerusalem council Peter stood up to defend salvation by grace for the Gentiles, and years later, in his last letter, he calls Paul ‘our beloved brother’ and honours the wisdom God gave him. The rebuke had not broken their fellowship; it had been received. Humility, truth and love outlasted the conflict.
